newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Grounds for optimism in New Zealand, says broker.
newsitem.headline: Grounds for optimism in New Zealand, says broker.

text.p: Auckland share broker Cavill White Securities said in its September quarter economic report on Wednesday there were grounds for optimism for markets.
Performance would depend on two triggers -- declining interest rates and the return of a centre-right government in the October 12 general election.
"On both counts there are grounds for optimism," Cavill White's Don Turkington said.
"Both seem much more likely now than they did three months ago. They could be the precursors to a sustained period of low-inflationary growth and market strength."
Despite persistent inflation, especially in the non-traded and non-competitive sectors, there was room for further falls in interest rates.

On the political front, the emergence of smaller centre-right parties, the Christian Coalition and ACT, made the formation of a viable coalition centred on the conservative ruling National Party a real possibility, he said.
Such a coalition would be highly positive for financial markets.

"The alternative to a National coalition victory in October is almost too awful to contemplate but should not be discounted," Turkington said. "A left-wing coalition would fundamentally change the economic course of New Zealand with equities, bonds and currency markets all likely to suffer."

"Should interest rates fall and a National coalition win on October 12, the performance of both New Zealand bonds and equities could be outstanding," he said. "For investors prepared to accept some political risk, we recommend investment now."
The gloom in business sentiment in June reflected not only political concerns but a marked slowing of the economy.
Cavill White does not expect the Reserve Bank to indicate an easing of policy in its six monthly economic projections on Friday.
However, it said the current interest rate structure did not appear sustainable.
"The result may be that the bond market continues to rally while the Reserve Bank does very little."
However, a rally in U.S. rates may stymie a local rally.
The New Zealand dollar was over-valued by almost any yardstick but would remain high while real interest rates held up. The currency was vulnerable to the election of a left-wing government.
A sharp rise in government spending would mean a targeted surplus of 2.9 percent of GDP would be difficult to achieve.
